A. $30 million
B. $40 million
C. $45 million
D. $50 million

questions.explanation: From Table 1, total 2023 revenue = $150 million. From Bar Chart 1, Laptops = 30% of total. Laptops revenue = 30% × $150M = 0.30 × 150 = $45 million.

| Year | Revenue |

BAR CHART 1: Revenue Share by Product Category in 2023 (% of total 2023 revenue)
| Category      | Share |
|---------------|-------|
| Smartphones   | 40%   |
| Laptops       | 30%   |
| Accessories   | 20%   |
| Smart Home    | 10%   |

By what percentage did total revenue increase from 2020 to 2022? Enter your answer to the nearest whole number percent.
questions.explanation:
Revenue in 2020 = $96M; Revenue in 2022 = $135M.
Percent change = (New − Old) / Old × 100 = (135 − 96) / 96 × 100 = 39/96 × 100 = 40.625% ≈ 41%.
The question asks to the nearest whole number, so the answer is 41.
questions.trap: Students compute (135 − 96)/135 × 100 = 28.9% ≈ 29%, dividing by the NEW value (2022) instead of the ORIGINAL value (2020). Percent change always uses the original as the base.

[SET 3 — RIVER COUNTY POPULATION STUDY]

TABLE 2: Population by City (in thousands)
BAR CHART 2: Percentage of Population Aged 65+ in 2023 by City

|------------|------------|
| Alderton   | 15%        |
| Brentville | 20%        |
| Clarksburg | 12%        |
| Dunmore    | 25%        |

Which city experienced the largest absolute increase in total population from 2015 to 2023?

A. Alderton
B. Brentville
C. Clarksburg
D. Dunmore
E. Both Alderton and Brentville equally
options: E. Both Alderton and Brentville equally
questions.explanation:
Absolute increases from 2015 to 2023:
- Alderton: 96 − 80 = 16,000
- Brentville: 132 − 120 = 12,000
- Clarksburg: 78 − 60 = 18,000
- Dunmore: 40 − 40 = 0
Largest absolute increase: Clarksburg at 18,000.
questions.trap: Students assume the largest starting population (Brentville, 120K) or highest 2023 population (Brentville, 132K) also has the largest increase. Largest absolute change requires computing the difference for each city — Clarksburg's 18,000 increase beats Alderton's 16,000 and Brentville's 12,000.

Select ALL cities in which the absolute number of residents aged 65+ in 2023 exceeded 14,000.

A. Alderton
B. Brentville
C. Clarksburg
D. Dunmore
questions.explanation:
Calculate 65+ count for each city using 2023 populations:
- Alderton: 15% × 96,000 = 14,400 > 14,000 ✓
- Brentville: 20% × 132,000 = 26,400 > 14,000 ✓
- Clarksburg: 12% × 78,000 = 9,360 < 14,000 ✗
- Dunmore: 25% × 40,000 = 10,000 < 14,000 ✗

Although Dunmore has the highest percentage (25%), its small total population makes the absolute count only 10,000. Cities A and B qualify.
questions.trap: Students select Dunmore (D) because it has the highest percentage (25%), not realizing that 25% of a small population (40,000) yields only 10,000 residents — less than the 14,000 threshold. Absolute count = percentage × base, and the base matters.

questions.question:
Use the following data for this question:

[SET 4 — NATIONAL BASKETBALL LEAGUE STATS: Team Performance]

TABLE 3: Season Records for Selected Teams
LINE GRAPH: Eagles' Monthly Win Totals
| Month    | Wins |
|----------|------|
| October  | 6    |
| November | 10   |
| December | 9    |
| January  | 11   |
| February | 9    |
| March    | 9    |

Based on the Line Graph, what was the Eagles' win percentage in November? (Win percentage = wins in that month ÷ games played in that month × 100. Assume the Eagles played the same number of games each month: 82 ÷ 6, rounded to the nearest whole number.)

Enter your answer as a percentage rounded to the nearest whole number.
questions.explanation:
Total games = 82; months = 6. Games per month = 82 ÷ 6 ≈ 13.67, rounded to 14 games per month (using nearest whole number as stated, except Oct may vary; standard is 14 for November in an 82-game season).

For consistency with the problem's instruction: 82 ÷ 6 ≈ 13.67 → 14 games per month (rounded to nearest whole).
November wins = 10 (from Line Graph).
Win % = 10/14 × 100 = 71.43% ≈ 71%.

Alternative: using exactly 82/6 = 13.67 games, win% = 10/13.67 × 100 = 73.2% ≈ 73%.

The intended calculation: 10 / (82/6) × 100 = 10 × 6/82 × 100 = 60/82 × 100 = 73.2% ≈ 73%.
questions.trap: Students round the games per month to 14 first, then compute 10/14 × 100 = 71.4% ≈ 71%, getting a different answer. The cleaner approach is to not round intermediate steps: use 82/6 exactly, giving 10/(82/6) = 60/82 ≈ 73%.

headers: | Games Played | Wins | Losses | Points For (avg/game) | Points Against (avg/game) |

Select ALL months in which the Eagles' win total was strictly above the team's average monthly wins for the season.

B. November
C. December
D. January
E. February
questions.explanation:
From the Line Graph, Eagles' total wins = 6+10+9+11+9+9 = 54 (consistent with Table 3).
Months = 6, so average monthly wins = 54 ÷ 6 = 9.0.

Months STRICTLY above 9:
- October: 6 < 9 ✗
- November: 10 > 9 ✓
- December: 9 = 9 ✗ (not strictly above)
- January: 11 > 9 ✓
- February: 9 = 9 ✗ (not strictly above)
- March: 9 = 9 ✗

Only November and January exceed the average.
questions.trap: Students include December, February, and March because they are 'at or above' average, missing the word 'strictly.' The question says strictly above, which excludes months equal to the mean (9). Only months with more than 9 wins qualify.

Which department had the greatest total number of patient admissions across all four years (2020–2023)?

A. Cardiology
B. Orthopedics
C. Neurology
D. General Surgery
E. Pediatrics
questions.explanation:
Sum of all four years per department:
- Cardiology: 4,800+5,100+5,400+5,700 = 21,000
- Orthopedics: 3,200+3,400+3,600+3,800 = 14,000
- Neurology: 2,100+2,300+2,500+2,400 = 9,300
- General Surgery: 6,500+6,200+6,800+7,200 = 26,700

Largest total: General Surgery at 26,700.
questions.trap: Students look only at 2023 values (the most recent year) and may compare Cardiology (5,700) vs General Surgery (7,200) without summing all years. For cumulative totals, all rows must be added — General Surgery consistently dominates.

questions.explanation:
Total 2020 population = 290,000. The 20% threshold = 0.20 × 290,000 = 58,000.
- Downtown: 58,000 — exactly at 20%, does NOT exceed ✗
- Midtown: 72,000 > 58,000 ✓
- Northshore: 60,000 > 58,000 ✓
- Eastside: 50,000 < 58,000 ✗
- Southgate: 50,000 < 58,000 ✗
Only Midtown (B) and Northshore (C) strictly exceed 20% of the total.
questions.trap: Students include Downtown (A) because 58,000 = 20% — they misread 'exceeded' as 'equaled or exceeded.' The word 'exceeded' means strictly greater than, so Downtown, at exactly 20%, does not qualify.

Use the following data for this question:

[SET 7 — CITY OF LAKEWOOD: Demographics & Housing]

TABLE 5: Population by District (in thousands)
PIE CHART 3: 2020 Housing Type Distribution (% of all housing units in Lakewood)
| Housing Type  | Percentage |
|---------------|------------|
| Single Family | 42%        |
| Apartments    | 35%        |
| Condos        | 15%        |
| Other         | 8%         |
Total housing units in 2020: 125,000

In 2020, how many persons per housing unit were there in Lakewood, on average? Enter your answer rounded to the nearest hundredth (e.g., 2.35).
questions.explanation:
Total population in 2020 = 290,000 (from Table 5 TOTAL row).
Total housing units in 2020 = 125,000 (from Pie Chart note).
Persons per unit = 290,000 / 125,000 = 2.32.
questions.trap: Students use 2015 population (260,000) divided by 125,000 = 2.08, mixing years. Or they use the pie chart percentages to compute something unrelated. The population figure must come from the 2020 TOTAL row in Table 5, and the housing unit figure comes from the pie chart note — two different data sources combined correctly.

Column A: Percentage increase in total grants (all departments) from 2019 to 2023
Column B: Percentage increase in total papers published from 2019 to 2023
options: C. The two quantities are equal
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
questions.trap: Students compare the absolute increases: Column A increased by $36M and Column B by 140 papers. Since the units differ and 140 > 36, students may incorrectly choose B. The question asks for PERCENTAGE increases, not absolute increases. The percent calculation requires dividing by the original value in each case.

BAR CHART 4: Annual Research Grants Received by Department (in $ millions)
LINE GRAPH 3: Annual Published Research Papers (all departments combined)
| Year | Papers Published |
|------|------------------|
| 2019 | 420              |
| 2020 | 450              |
| 2021 | 480              |
| 2022 | 510              |
| 2023 | 560              |

Across all five years (2019–2023), what was the average funding per published paper for the university as a whole? Express your answer in thousands of dollars, rounded to the nearest whole number (e.g., 47 means $47,000).
questions.trap: Students compute the average grants per year ($344M / 5 = $68.8M) and average papers per year (2,420/5 = 484), then divide $68.8M / 484 = $142,149 — which coincidentally gives the same answer. However, the correct single-step approach is total grants / total papers, not average/average. These happen to agree here because dividing numerator and denominator by the same constant (5 years) cancels out. A more dangerous trap: students use only 2023 data ($88M / 560 = $157,143) and report 157.

questions.question:
Use the following data for this question:

[SET 8 — BRANDFORD UNIVERSITY: Research Funding & Output]

BAR CHART 4: Annual Research Grants Received by Department (in $ millions)
LINE GRAPH 3: Annual Published Research Papers (all departments combined)
| Year | Papers Published |
|------|------------------|
| 2019 | 420              |
| 2020 | 450              |
| 2021 | 480              |
| 2022 | 510              |
| 2023 | 560              |

Assume that total papers published each year are distributed across departments in proportion to their share of total grants in that year. Select ALL years in which the implied number of papers published by the Engineering department was greater than 100.

A. 2019
B. 2020
C. 2021
D. 2022
E. 2023
questions.explanation:
For each year, Engineering's implied papers = (Engineering grants / Total grants) × Total papers:

2019: 16/52 × 420 = 6,720/52 = 129.2 > 100 ✓
2020: 18/60 × 450 = 8,100/60 = 135.0 > 100 ✓
2021: 20/67 × 480 = 9,600/67 = 143.3 > 100 ✓
2022: 22/77 × 510 = 11,220/77 = 145.7 > 100 ✓
2023: 25/88 × 560 = 14,000/88 = 159.1 > 100 ✓

All five years show Engineering publishing more than 100 papers under the proportional assumption. Despite the changing grant share (28.4%–30.8%) and growing paper totals, Engineering always clears the 100-paper threshold.
questions.trap: Students estimate Engineering's share as 'roughly 30%' and then check 30% × 420 = 126 without computing each year individually, assuming some years will fall below 100 due to smaller grant shares. In fact, Engineering's share ranges from 28.4% to 30.8% across years, and with paper totals of 420–560, the product always exceeds 100. The extreme-hard element is the multi-step computation for each of five years, combined with the assumption stated in the question that must be applied correctly.
